title: New York City Bar Formal Opinion 2006-3: Outsourcing Legal Support Services Overseas
pub: Association of the Bar of the City of New York
author: Association of the Bar of the City of New York · Committee on Professional and Judicial Ethics

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal outsourcing: Commercial growth need not advance workers
st.an: The excerpt defines substantive versus administrative outsourced legal support and supplies historical context, but does not assess whether outsourcing’s commercial growth advances workers’ substantive work, professional capital, autonomy or status.
qs: 4   This opinion concerns outsourcing of “substantive legal support services,” which include legal research, drafting, due diligence reports, patent and trademark work, review of transactional and litigation documents, and drafting contracts, pleadings, or memoranda of law.

This is distinguished from “administrative legal support services,” which include transcription of voice files from depositions, trials and hearings; accounting support in the preparation of timesheets and billing materials; paralegal and clerical support for file management; litigation support graphics; and data entry for marketing, conflicts, and contact management.

st.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s core distinction: outsourcing preserves the lawyer’s professional responsibility and duty to supervise, while the required degree of supervision varies with the circumstances. Its disciplinary framework also ties responsibility for specific misconduct to ordering, directing or knowingly ratifying that conduct rather than imposing automatic liability for every delegated error.

st.t: Cross-border outsourcing: Oversight follows the provider chain
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s proposition that cross-border outsourcing is permissible but leaves professional responsibility with the retaining lawyer. It conditions outsourcing on rigorous supervision, competence, confidentiality, conflict safeguards, appropriate billing and context-dependent client consent, while rejecting supervision as an automatic answer to unauthorized-practice concerns.
qs: But at the same time, to avoid aiding the unauthorized practice of law, the lawyer must at every step shoulder complete responsibility for the non-lawyer’s work.

st.t: Outsourcing fees: Delegation cannot justify double recovery
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: outsourcing does not relieve the lawyer of professional responsibility, and outsourcing charges cannot produce an undisclosed markup or double recovery. It requires complete responsibility and supervision while limiting client charges, absent a contrary agreement, to direct cost plus reasonably allocated associated overhead.
qs: But at the same time, to avoid aiding the unauthorized practice of law, the lawyer must at every step shoulder complete responsibility for the non-lawyer’s work.

Absent a specific agreement with the client to the contrary, the lawyer should charge the client no more than the direct cost associated with outsourcing, plus a reasonable allocation of overhead expenses directly associated with providing that service.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s human-led work-redesign proposition by permitting delegation of substantive legal tasks while keeping supervision, competence, client relationships and professional accountability with the lawyer. Its detailed ethical conditions reinforce the importance of oversight, though it concerns overseas human outsourcing rather than AI and therefore does not establish AI’s jagged capabilities or task-level performance.

kp.k: Overseas outsourcing is ethically permissible subject to safeguards
kp.d: The Committee's August 2006 opinion interprets the then-applicable New York Code of Professional Responsibility, rather than addressing AI. It permits overseas outsourcing of substantive legal support subject to supervision, competence, confidentiality, conflicts safeguards, appropriate billing and, where necessary, advance client consent. Its scope includes foreign lawyers not admitted in any U.S. jurisdiction and laypeople, both treated as non-lawyers for this analysis.
qs: A New York lawyer may ethically outsource legal support services overseas to a non-lawyer

This opinion concerns outsourcing of “substantive legal support services,” which include legal research, drafting, due diligence reports, patent and trademark work, review of transactional and litigation documents, and drafting contracts, pleadings, or memoranda of law.

kp.k: Cost and efficiency motivate delegation of substantive legal work
kp.d: The opinion describes corporate legal departments and law firms turning to overseas outsourcing to reduce costs and improve operations. It presents this as a developing practice, supported by contemporary reporting, rather than a quantified finding about savings or employment effects. Quoting EC 3-6, it identifies economic benefits of delegation while retaining the lawyer's direct client relationship, supervision and complete professional responsibility.
qs: Much more recently, outsourcing overseas has begun to command attention in the legal profession, as corporate legal departments and law firms endeavor to reduce costs and manage operations more efficiently.
This delegation enables a lawyer to render legal service more economically and efficiently.

kp.k: Lawyers retain responsibility for scope, review and work quality
kp.d: The Committee makes supervision central to avoiding assistance in unauthorized practice, without accepting that every task becomes permissible simply because an attorney supervises it. Lawyers must define the assignment using professional judgment and vet the resulting work. The Committee expressly agrees with a Los Angeles County ethics opinion requiring independent checks of accuracy, relevance and completeness, and revision before court submission where necessary.
qs: But at the same time, to avoid aiding the unauthorized practice of law, the lawyer must at every step shoulder complete responsibility for the non-lawyer’s work.
In short, the lawyer must, by applying professional skill and judgment, first set the appropriate scope for the non-lawyer’s work and then vet the non-lawyer’s work and ensure its quality.
This committee does not go so far.

kp.k: Remote supervision requires diligence and ongoing communication
kp.d: The opinion connects adequate supervision to competent representation under DR 6-101. Physical separation requires particular vigilance. Recommended steps include investigating intermediaries, obtaining workers' résumés, checking references, interviewing prospective workers about assignment suitability, and communicating throughout the assignment. The quoted supervisory rule makes the appropriate degree of oversight depend on experience, workload and likely ethical problems.
qs: Given these considerations and given the hurdles imposed by the physical separation between the New York lawyer and the overseas non-lawyer, the New York lawyer must be both vigilant and creative in discharging the duty to supervise.

The degree of supervision required is that which is reasonable under the circumstances, taking into account factors such as the experience of the person whose work is being supervised, the amount of work involved in a particular matter, and the likelihood that ethical problems might arise in the course of working on the matter.

kp.k: Supervisory responsibility extends to firms and individual lawyers
kp.d: The Committee interprets DR 1-104(C) and (D) as covering both the firm and individual lawyer despite different language concerning workers at the firm and workers retained by a lawyer. It rejects an interpretation that would exempt the firm from responsibility for overseas workers. The cited individual-responsibility provisions address ordering or knowingly ratifying misconduct and supervisory knowledge, including what reasonable management should have discovered while remedial action remained possible.
qs: Nonetheless, the Committee believes that these two phrases were intended to be equivalent.

To conclude otherwise and make the individual lawyer, but not the law firm, responsible for supervising the overseas non-lawyer would be difficult to justify and could also easily lead to untoward results.

kp.k: Confidential outsourcing requires informed consent and protective measures
kp.d: Where an assignment requires disclosing client confidences or secrets to an overseas non-lawyer, the Committee calls for informed advance consent. Lawyers must consider differences in foreign confidentiality laws and traditions, without assuming that foreign protections are always weaker. Suggested protections include access restrictions, confidentiality contracts with breach remedies and periodic reminders.
qs: We conclude that if the outsourcing assignment requires the lawyer to disclose client confidences or secrets to the overseas non-lawyer, then the lawyer should secure the client’s informed consent in advance.

Measures that New York lawyers may take to help preserve client confidences and secrets when outsourcing overseas include restricting access to confidences and secrets, contractual provisions addressing confidentiality and remedies in the event of breach, and periodic reminders regarding confidentiality.
We do not mean to suggest that confidentiality laws and traditions overseas always provide less protection than in New York.

kp.k: Conflict inquiries should cover intermediaries and overseas workers
kp.d: The opinion distinguishes the formal obligation to add incoming lawyers' prior engagements to conflicts systems from prior guidance that does not impose the same obligation for incoming non-lawyers. Nevertheless, outsourcing lawyers should investigate intermediaries' conflict procedures and tracking, ordinarily ask both intermediaries and workers about services for adverse parties, and follow up as needed. These inquiries must also respect other clients' confidentiality.
qs: As a threshold matter, the outsourcing New York lawyer should ask the intermediary, which employs or engages the overseas non-lawyer, about its conflict-checking procedures and about how it tracks work performed for other clients.

The outsourcing New York lawyer should also ordinarily ask both the intermediary and the non-lawyer performing the legal support service whether either is performing, or has performed, services for any parties adverse to the lawyer’s client.

kp.k: Outsourcing charges default to cost plus attributable overhead
kp.d: The Committee treats overseas non-lawyer work as legal support rather than legal services and says its cost should not be included in the lawyer's legal fees. Absent a specific contrary client agreement, charges should not exceed direct outsourcing costs plus a reasonable allocation of directly associated overhead. The consent discussion additionally requires informed advance consent for billing on a basis other than cost.
qs: By definition, the non-lawyer performing legal support services overseas is not performing legal services.
It is thus inappropriate for the New York lawyer to include the cost of outsourcing in his or her legal fees.

Absent a specific agreement with the client to the contrary, the lawyer should charge the client no more than the direct cost associated with outsourcing, plus a reasonable allocation of overhead expenses directly associated with providing that service.

kp.k: Client disclosure and consent depend on outsourcing circumstances
kp.d: The Committee does not require automatic notification for every overseas non-lawyer assignment, distinguishing these often limited roles from temporary or contract lawyers. Additional considerations include significant participation, such as an important document review staffed by several non-lawyers; sharing confidences or secrets; a client expectation that only firm employees will work on the matter; and non-cost billing. The opinion expressly identifies confidential disclosure and non-cost billing as requiring informed advance consent.
qs: Non-lawyers often play more limited roles in matters than contract or temporary lawyers do.
non-lawyers will play a significant role in the matter, e.g., several non-lawyers are being hired to do an important document review;
the client expects that only personnel employed by the law firm will handle the matter;
in which case the client’s informed advance consent is needed.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The opinion makes no claims about AI. In its own domain, the Committee claims that overseas outsourcing of substantive legal support can support more economical and efficient legal services and is ethically permissible subject to safeguards.
pts.d: The New York City Bar Committee on Professional and Judicial Ethics describes overseas outsourcing as attracting interest from law firms and corporate legal departments seeking lower costs and greater operational efficiency. Its principal conclusion is conditional ethical permission, not a prediction about technology or employment: New York lawyers may delegate substantive support work to overseas non-lawyers while retaining professional responsibility, rigorously supervising and checking the work, protecting confidentiality, addressing conflicts, billing appropriately, and securing advance client consent where necessary. Covered work includes research, document review, drafting, and due diligence. The opinion does not claim that outsourcing permits independent legal representation by overseas non-lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The support is primarily legal and ethical authority, supplemented by contemporary reporting about outsourcing; no quantitative assessment of savings, quality, or employment effects is provided.
pts.d: The Committee grounds its conclusions in the then-applicable New York Code of Professional Responsibility, Judiciary Law § 478, Spivak v. Sachs, and prior city, state, ABA, and other jurisdictions’ ethics opinions. It expressly endorses the Los Angeles County Bar’s requirement to independently check outsourced work. Newspaper and professional-publication citations support the background account of increasing outsourcing interest. These are normative interpretations and qualitative observations, not empirical findings about measured performance. The opinion neither studies AI nor supplies evidence that these conclusions apply to AI systems.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: This is an August 2006 interpretation of New York’s then-applicable ethics code, with ongoing conditions for outsourcing rather than a forecast.
pts.d: Permission depends on supervision throughout the assignment and lawyer review of the resulting work. Physical separation calls for particular vigilance, with suggested measures including background and reference checks, advance interviews, and communication during the assignment. Sharing client confidences or secrets requires informed advance consent. Significant non-lawyer participation and a client’s expectation that only firm personnel will work on the matter can also alter disclosure and consent requirements. Absent a specific contrary agreement, charges should not exceed direct outsourcing costs plus a reasonable allocation of directly associated overhead; billing other than at cost requires informed advance consent. The analysis concerns substantive, not administrative, legal support and should not be presented as a statement of current rules.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The opinion addresses New York lawyers and firms, corporate legal departments, overseas support workers and intermediaries, and clients whose work and information are outsourced.
pts.d: Lawyers and firms gain a permissible means of delegating support work but retain supervision, competence, confidentiality, conflicts, billing, and consent responsibilities. Corporate legal departments are identified alongside firms as seeking efficiency and cost reductions. Overseas providers include laypeople and foreign lawyers not admitted in any U.S. jurisdiction, treated as non-lawyers for this analysis; they may perform supervised substantive support rather than independently provide the New York lawyer’s legal services. Clients receive safeguards concerning work quality, confidential information, charges, and participation decisions. Intermediaries are subjects of due diligence and inquiries into conflicts procedures. The Committee does not predict displacement of domestic lawyers, changes in staffing structures, or effects on unmet civil legal need.
